harvest_window: Late September at WSU Mount Vernon (9/29 mean, 2002-2017); late October in England
disease_notes: Susceptible to fireblight as a young tree and to powdery mildew; latent virus can cause small, cracked, heavily russeted fruit. Poor cold hardiness - trees died at Montana WARC after the 2020 cold event. Semi-alternate bearing at WSU.
description: A full bittersweet from Somerset and a probable parent of Dabinett. WSU Mount Vernon measures 0.42% tannin, 0.25% malic acid, pH 4.31, SG 1.056, 13.8 Brix and 232 mL/lb juice yield, and its sensory panel describes a golden amber juice with barnyard notes, citrus, pronounced bitterness and a tannic finish, recommended for blending rather than standing alone. Well suited to a maritime PNW site, with the caveat that its tannins are hard.
discrepancies: Bloom: WSU 5/19 puts it in group 4 on the Mount Vernon range (4/19-5/29); RHS/Cummins call it group 5 (late). Recommend 4 - WSU is the local climate. Vigor: Cummins says low vigor, Montana WARC growers say moderate; recommend moderate (extension over nursery). Tannin: WSU 0.42% and Long Ashton 0.40% agree, but Montana WARC reports 1.05% by the Lowenthal-Permanganate method, which reads high and is not comparable. Harvest order: at Mount Vernon it ripens 9/29, two weeks BEFORE Michelin, inverting the English sequence.

origin: USA, Paris, Oxford County, Maine, c. 1790; DNA profiling gives parentage as Hunt Russet x Blue Pearmain
harvest_window: Very late - mid to late October, picked as hard frost approaches; keeps into spring
disease_notes: Good general disease and insect resistance; reported resistant to apple scab and fireblight with strong cedar-apple rust resistance. Hardy to zone 4.
description: Correctly Black Oxford, found as a seedling on the Valentine farm in Paris, Maine around 1790. Medium, round, deep purple-black fruit with greenish-white flesh, dense and balanced in sugar and acid, hard off the tree but sweetening in storage and improving through winter. Used fresh, for pies and sauce, and notably for late-season cider.
discrepancies: Bloom: Fedco describes early-to-midseason bloom, Cummins assigns bloom group 4 (mid-late). Recommend 4 because it is an explicit rating on a defined scale rather than prose, but treat as uncertain. Not present in the WSU database (77 cultivars), so there is no PNW trial data on bloom, harvest or juice chemistry; the sweet cider classification comes from a nursery catalog only and the apple is better described as dual-purpose.

origin: France/England - Isle of Wight, introduced from Normandy in 1817 but older in origin
harvest_window: Picked late; ripens December-January and stores at least to March in Isle of Wight records. No WSU harvest date recorded.
disease_notes: Very resistant to canker and mildew (Isle of Wight records). No WSU disease observations recorded.
description: Almost certainly Isle of Wight Pippin, which WSU Mount Vernon holds on G935 and classifies as a bittersweet cider apple of France/England origin - confirming the orchard's record of it as a cider variety. Smallish flat fruit, yellow with an orange flush and some russet, green-tinged flesh, slightly sweet with good bouquet; it flowers early but matures very late. WSU has recorded no juice chemistry, bloom date, harvest date or sensory evaluation for it, so the trial entry establishes identity and class but nothing quantitative.
discrepancies: Classification: WSU lists it as bittersweet; the Isle of Wight variety records describe it purely as a late-storing dessert apple. Recommend BSW per WSU, which is the higher-priority source and matches the orchard's own use. Acidity low and tannin medium are inferred from that bittersweet classification (>0.20% tannin, <0.45% acid), not measured - no juice analysis exists for this cultivar. Bloom group 1 comes from the Isle of Wight description of early flowering; WSU has no bloom date.

origin: France, Normandy (Manche, commune of Nehou), before the late 19th century
harvest_window: Early - mid September at WSU Mount Vernon (9/17 mean); poor keeper, press within about two weeks
disease_notes: No specific susceptibilities documented; thin-skinned, soft-fleshed fruit bruises easily and stores poorly. WSU recorded no productivity rating.
description: An old Normandy full bittersweet, small to medium and conic, yellow with a pink blush. WSU Mount Vernon measures 0.34% tannin, 0.32% malic acid, pH 4.10, SG 1.056, 14.0 Brix and 216 mL/lb juice yield - among the more tannic bittersweets in the collection and a genuine standalone cider apple, though it is not yet sensory-evaluated. It ties for the earliest bloom date in the entire WSU collection (4/19, with Golden Russet and Hewes Crab), which is the single most important planting consideration for it.
discrepancies: Acidity: nursery descriptions call it sweet with only marginal tartness, but WSU measures 0.32% malic - at the top of the bittersweet band and noticeably sharper than Michelin (0.27%) or Sweet Coppin (0.20%). Recommend low for band consistency (<0.45%) while noting the nursery framing understates it. Bloom: no nursery source flags the frost exposure; WSU's 4/19 date is the earliest in a 40-day range, so bloom group 1 is well supported and is a real spring-frost risk in Port Angeles.

origin: USA, northeastern US (Lake Champlain region); origin obscure, described in Beach, The Apples of New York (1905)
harvest_window: Ripens in succession from late August into October; needs more than two pickings
disease_notes: Described as hardy and healthy; no specific susceptibilities recorded in any source consulted.
description: A large greenish-yellow late-summer to fall apple with tender juicy flesh and brisk acidity, good for dessert and excellent for culinary use. The tree is a good grower, hardy, moderately long-lived, bears young and crops reliably. In a cider blend it would act as a sharp - high acid, negligible tannin - rather than as a purpose-bred cider variety.
discrepancies: Identity is the main problem: Beach records Champlain as of obscure origin and possibly identical to Sour Bough, Summer Pippin or Tart Bough, with synonyms Calkins' Pippin, Geneva Pearmain and Walworth - so the name may not map to a single cultivar. The two modern nursery descriptions both trace back to Beach rather than being independent, and it is absent from the WSU database, so there is no PNW trial data. Bearing: Beach says crops biennially or almost annually; recommended moderate as the midpoint.

description: No authoritative record of an apple under this name was found. Checked and absent from: the WSU Mount Vernon Cultivar Performance Database (all 77 cultivars), Pomiferous, Orange Pippin, and French nursery and conservatory variety catalogues. The name is most likely a garbled or local rendering of another cultivar - plausible candidates are Belle de Boskoop (Netherlands 1856, triploid, high-acid, rated as a single-varietal cider apple) or one of the French Belle varieties such as Belle de Tours, Belle Fille Normande or Belle Fille de la Manche. Treat the orchard's tree as unidentified until it is compared against a reference collection or DNA-fingerprinted; MOFGA's Maine Heritage Orchard runs such a project jointly with WSU.
discrepancies: Not a conflict between sources but a total absence of them - no source at any priority tier documents this name. Every field is left null rather than inferred from the candidate cultivars, since choosing among Belle de Boskoop and the French Belle varieties would change ploidy, acid and season completely.

origin: USA, New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva NY; crossed by Richard Wellington in 1924 (Wolf River x Malus niedzwetzkyana), selected 1935 as Station 4840, introduced 1938
harvest_window: Late - October, with Cummins placing it around early November in New York (about 49 days after McIntosh)
disease_notes: Resistant to fireblight and very resistant to apple scab; exceptionally cold hardy (zones 3-7). Distinctive red wood and pink blossoms.
description: A red-fleshed Wolf River x Malus niedzwetzkyana cross, large with dark red russet-netted skin and firm crimson flesh. The juice is tart, aromatic and astringent - too sharp to eat but valued by cidermakers for the ruby colour and tart-dry structure it contributes. Grown as a colour and acid component rather than a base variety.
discrepancies: Bloom: Cummins assigns bloom group 3, but several independent nurseries describe Redfield as one of the first apples to bloom each year, which would be group 1-2. Recommended 3 because it is an explicit rating on a defined scale, but plant on the assumption of early bloom and frost exposure until confirmed. Harvest: Cummins gives roughly November 3 in NY while other catalogs say September-October; recommended a late-October framing that spans both. Class: Cummins classifies it Sharp while several nurseries call the resulting cider bittersweet; recommended SH, since the astringency comes largely from anthocyanins rather than the tannin the English classes measure. Absent from the WSU database - no PNW trial data.

origin: England, Gloucester, early 1700s; raised from seed by the lawyer William Ashmead
harvest_window: Late - mid to late October; stores and improves into winter. No WSU harvest date recorded.
disease_notes: Moderate disease resistance; blooms late enough to escape most frosts. WSU records standard bearing, upright-spreading habit and a low blind-wood rating of 1.0. Poor cold hardiness - trees were lost at Montana WARC to the 2020 cold event. Triploid, so it needs two diploid pollinators and contributes no usable pollen.
description: A small to mid-sized russet with honey-green skin, an orange blush and dense, nutty, intensely aromatic flesh with high acidity. WSU Mount Vernon holds it on G935 and classifies it as a sharp cider apple. University trials in Vermont and Ontario found it among the highest-sugar cultivars tested at 18.3 Brix (about SG 1.075), with titratable acidity well above common dessert cultivars and the only cultivar in that trial with yeast-assimilable nitrogen above the 140-350 mg/L optimum - unusually favourable fermentation chemistry.
discrepancies: Bearing: WSU records alternate bearing as No, against a widespread reputation as a shy and irregular cropper. Recommended low per WSU, the local trial. Class: recorded as SH per WSU rather than dessert, correcting the common nursery framing as a connoisseur eating apple - it is both, but the cider role is sharp. SG 1.075 is converted from the 18.3 Brix reported in the UVM/Guelph trials, not a directly published gravity, and WSU holds no juice chemistry for this cultivar at all. Bloom group 4 comes from RHS/Cummins; WSU has no bloom date, so unlike the other WSU cultivars here it is not locally calibrated.

origin: France, Yvetot, Normandy; raised by the nurseryman Legrand, first fruited 1872, named for pomologist Henri Michelin
harvest_window: Mid-October at WSU Mount Vernon (10/12 mean); mid-September in New York
disease_notes: Susceptible to apple scab, mildew, canker and especially fireblight - 50-90% tree mortality after seven years of severe natural fireblight infection in trial, and half the Montana growers who planted it removed it for fireblight. WSU records a blind-wood rating of 2.0 and semi-alternate bearing. This is the main risk for a humid maritime site.
description: The most widely planted bittersweet cider apple in England, small to medium, round, green-yellow with russet specks. WSU Mount Vernon measures pH 4.09, SG 1.048, 11.4 Brix and 166 mL/lb juice yield, with a semi-spur, semi-upright habit and the highest productivity rating (3.6) of the four WSU cultivars in this set. Its sensory panel calls it a golden amber juice with strong apple and berry aroma that can stand alone but benefits from blending - a dependable blending workhorse rather than a vintage single varietal.
discrepancies: Tannin: WSU measures 0.14%, Long Ashton 0.23%. WSU's own figure falls in the sweet band (<0.20%) yet WSU still classifies the cultivar bittersweet, so the single mean looks like the outlier rather than a real reclassification; recommended medium, which both classifications support. Bloom: WSU 5/12 maps to group 3 on the Mount Vernon range; RHS and BC Tree Fruit call it group 4 / mid-late. Recommended 3 per WSU. Harvest: WSU 10/12 versus Cummins' September 8 in New York - a five-week regional gap, and the WSU date is the one that applies to Port Angeles. Bearing: WSU semi-alternate against Salt Spring's claim of little trouble with biennialism; recommended moderate per WSU.

origin: England, Devon/Somerset (associated with Martock), early 18th century
harvest_window: Mid-October at WSU Mount Vernon (10/10 mean); fruit drops when ripe and does not store more than a few weeks
disease_notes: Susceptible to apple scab and powdery mildew. WSU records a blind-wood rating of 2.0, spreading habit, and the lowest bloom density (2.4) and productivity (2.7) of the four WSU cultivars in this set. Hardy to zone 5.
description: Correctly Sweet Coppin, a Devon-style pure sweet cider apple with soft white flesh, very low acid and very low tannin. WSU Mount Vernon measures 0.11% tannin, 0.20% malic acid, pH 4.03, SG 1.048, 11.3 Brix and 273 mL/lb juice yield - the highest juice yield of the four WSU cultivars here, which is what makes it valuable as the base and body of a blend despite modest sugar. Fruit drops readily at ripeness, so pick promptly.
discrepancies: Specific gravity: WSU measures 1.048, Fedco and AppleWise both advertise 1.052. Recommended 1.048 - WSU is measured trial data from the same maritime climate, and the nursery figure likely comes from English sources. Tannin: WSU 0.11% versus Long Ashton 0.14%; both are firmly in the sweet band so the difference does not matter. Bearing: Fedco says it tends toward biennialism and BC Tree Fruit flags biennial potential, while WSU records only semi-alternate; recommended moderate per WSU. Vigor: left null - no trial or extension source records tree vigour, only WSU's spreading growth habit.

origin: USA, probably near Washington, New Jersey, before 1804; carried to Tompkins County, New York in 1804 by Jacob Wycoff
harvest_window: Mid-season - around early October in New York (about 21 days after McIntosh); stores one to three months
disease_notes: Resistant to apple scab; susceptible to fireblight, perennial canker, cedar-apple rust and collar rot. Makes poor root growth, so it should be grafted onto a vigorous rootstock. Triploid and pollen-sterile - needs two diploid pollinators and will not pollinate others.
description: Also known as King or King of Tompkins County, a large, uniform, mostly red apple with yellow striping and crisp yellowish flesh of rich, aromatic flavour. Excellent both as a dessert apple and for cooking, best left to colour up fully on the tree, though it does not store as long as many heirlooms. In cider it contributes aroma and moderate acid rather than tannin. Absent from the WSU database, so no PNW trial data exists for it.
